THE FIRST KINGDOM Before there were kings, there was the Earth. Before there were kingdoms, there was the hearth. Before there were written laws, there were the rhythms of creation: the turning of the seasons, the fertility of the soil, the passage of the stars, the certainty of birth, and the inevitability of death. Humanity did not invent these things. We inherited them. We crowned kings, erected monuments, surveyed borders, and established laws. We built temples to the divine and palaces to the powerful. items.title: BREAKING: FAA Orders Nationwide Ground Stop Following Air Traffic Control Communications Failure
items.summary: Flights halted across the United States Friday afternoon as federal aviation officials investigate widespread communications problems. MIAMI, Okla. — November 13, 2026 | Miami News-Digest The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, November 13, temporarily suspending aircraft departures across the United States after a widespread communications failure affected the nation's air traffic control system. The emergency directive was issued for aviation safety reasons as federal technicians investigated problems affecting all 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers, which manage aircraft traveling between airports across the country. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the communications disruption and said FAA technicians were working to identify and resolve the problem. According to Reuters and the Associated Press, aircraft already airborne were permitted to continue flying and land at their destinations, while departing aircraft were instructed to remain on the ground. items.title: Bear Wrestling, $1 Swearing Fines, and Other Strange Oklahoma Laws Still on the Books
items.summary: From fortune-telling and cemetery bird eggs to Sunday car sales, Oklahoma's legal history contains some surprisingly unusual provisions. MIAMI, Okla. — Oklahoma is a state known for its colorful history, independent spirit, and occasionally peculiar traditions. However, some of its strangest stories are not found in museums, folklore, or dusty history books. They are written into the state's laws. Buried within the Oklahoma Statutes are provisions addressing everything from wrestling bears and charging for psychic readings to using religious names in casual conversation. Some are more than a century old, while others are surprisingly recent. Although many of these laws are rarely enforced, and some face serious constitutional obstacles, their continued presence offers an entertaining glimpse into Oklahoma's changing social values and legislative history. items.summary: Judicial compensation proposal carried an estimated $10 million price tag, while court-reporter shortages and questions about transparency continue to confront the state. By Miami News-Digest | November 5, 2026 OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahoma judges sought substantial salary increases through the state's judicial compensation process, but lawmakers rejected a proposed 17.58% raise earlier this year, bringing renewed attention to the competing demands of judicial compensation, taxpayer spending, and the performance of the state's court system. The Oklahoma Board on Judicial Compensation recommended the increase on September 16, 2025, citing comparatively low judicial salaries and the need to attract qualified candidates. Under the proposal, the Oklahoma Supreme Court chief justice's annual salary would have increased from $198,212 to approximately $233,062, while district judges would have received approximately $197,189, compared with their existing $167,703 salaries. Cleveland County District Judge Thad Balkman, then president of the Oklahoma Judges Association, estimated the proposal would cost approximately $10 million annually, covering 277 trial and appellate judges statewide. items.title: A Sacred Legacy: Historic Quapaw Crucifix Preserves More Than a Century of Native American Catholic Heritage in Miami
items.summary: A Sacred Legacy: Historic Quapaw Crucifix Preserves More Than a Century of Native American Catholic Heritage in Miami From a 19th-century mission on Quapaw land to Sacred Heart Catholic Church, a remarkable crucifix tells a story of faith, tribal leadership, sacrifice, and remembrance. By Miami News-Digest MIAMI, Okla. — Behind glass at Sacred Heart Catholic Church in Miami rests a remarkable piece of northeastern Oklahoma history: a wooden crucifix connected to St. Mary's of the Quapaws, a Catholic mission established in Indian Territory more than 130 years ago. Mounted against a dark blue background, the crucifix bears a small inscription identifying its origins: "Crucifix from St. Mary of the Quapaws, 1893–1927." Yet the religious artifact represents considerably more than the history of a church. It preserves a connection between generations of Quapaw families, the early development of Catholicism in northeastern Oklahoma, and a mission whose legacy extended far beyond its closing nearly a century ago. items.title: F.D.R. Second Bill of Rights
items.summary: EDITORIAL | MIAMI NEWS-DIGEST Franklin D. Roosevelt’s 1944 proposal for a “Second Bill of Rights” raised a question that remains unsettled: What does freedom mean when political rights exist on paper, but economic insecurity limits a citizen’s ability to exercise them in practice? By Miami News-Digest In January 1944, with the United States still fighting the Second World War, President Franklin D. Roosevelt placed before the country an idea that remains remarkably unsettled more than eight decades later. Americans, he argued, had inherited indispensable political rights—freedom of speech, freedom of worship, trial by jury, protection against unreasonable searches—but an industrial society had revealed another problem. A citizen could possess those liberties in law and still lack the practical independence necessary to exercise them. items.title: Oklahoma Saved $202 Million by Not Imprisoning Drug Users. Counties Got $37.5 Million.
items.summary: Voters told Oklahoma to send SQ 780 prison savings to county treatment. A 2025 report puts savings at $202.3 million and county investment at $37.5 million. Three words in the statute let lawmakers wait six years.
